answers.1: Most of it is already decided. House Bill 1009 (the page says its law number is Act 395) bans public high school students from using phones and similar devices for the whole school day, from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, unless a health or disability plan requires one. Georgia lawmakers in the House and Senate passed it, and Gov. Brian Kemp signed it on May 5, 2026. It takes effect Dec 31, 2026, and high schools must start the ban by July 1, 2027 at the latest. Some may start sooner. The details are still being decided: each school district and school writes its own policy by Jan 1 each year (how phones are stored, emergency messages, off-campus activities, what happens when students break the rules). Lawmakers could also change the law in a later session. Two things confused me. The home page lists this under 'What's being decided' even though it's already law. And the 'Decided now, and decided later' and 'Not known yet' headings had nothing under them.
answers.2: Not that I can see. The page says, as its own analysis, that the law sets aside no money and doesn't require families to pay for anything. So it gives no amount and no date for me. It doesn't say whether my district could ask families to buy anything for phone storage, or whether the schools' new work (staff time, phone storage) would end up costing me some other way. Each option has a 'who pays' label, but I couldn't see what it says without tapping. The page doesn't explain why it can't say more.
answers.3: According to the page, no money moves: the law sets aside no money and families don't have to pay. But schools must take on new work, like assigning staff and checking phone storage, with no money set aside for it. The page never says who pays for that or where that money comes from. The Georgia Department of Education must give schools guidance and technical support, but the page doesn't say any money comes with it.
answers.4: 1) Ask my school district how it will store phones, handle emergency messages, run off-campus activities and deal with students who break the rules. The home page says to do this before Jan 1, 2027, when district policies are due, and policies get updated by Jan 1 every year after that. 2) If my district holds a family workshop, question-and-answer session or town hall, ask there. No dates are given. 3) Tell state lawmakers in the General Assembly whether to keep or change the law. No deadline is given, and the page doesn't say when they meet next. 4) Check my school's handbook or website for the rules, especially since my kid's school may start before July 1, 2027. The page leaves two gaps. It gives no phone numbers, emails or meetings for my district, lawmakers or the governor, so I'd have to find those myself. And it only tells me to ask the district questions. It doesn't say whether the district takes parents' input or votes on its policy at a public meeting.
answers.5: The Arguments tab explains them. 'Supported' means the records or studies they found back the claim up. 'Supported, with limits' means it's backed up, with limits named on the card. 'Uncertain' means nothing they found settles it yet. 'Not mainly factual' means it's mostly about what's fair or right, not about facts. Some things confused me. Two 'against' cards show 'Supported' and 'Uncertain' at the same time, and they don't say which part each label goes with. The page says 'one rule sets every evidence label,' but the 'This page's exact rule' heading had nothing under it. And the top of the page says 'Reader-first update; checks pending' and that no person reviewed it, but I don't know what those checks are.
answers.6: For: 'The ban will help students learn.' Supporters say fewer distractions mean students learn more. A Florida study found better test scores in the ban's second year, but there are no Georgia high school results yet. It's labeled 'Supported, with limits.' Against: 'Families lose direct contact with students during the school day.' Parents have to go through the school to reach their kids, and opponents say a phone can be critical in an emergency. The page says its sources have no data on emergency safety.

seemed_to_favor: Mostly even. It gives three reasons for and three against in the same format and says it doesn't recommend an option. Two things leaned a little toward the law. First, it quotes five supporters and only one opponent. The page admits this and says it reflects who its sources quoted, not how many people agree. Second, in the 'each side's own words' part, the supporter is the State School Superintendent talking about learning and mental health. The opponent is one teacher saying older teachers don't want confrontation. That makes the other side sound weaker than the emergency-contact worry I actually have as a parent. On the other hand, two of the three 'for' cards are labeled 'Uncertain', so it didn't oversell the law.
hardest: Question 3 (whose money moves). The page says the law sets aside no money and families don't pay, but schools still have to assign staff and store phones with no money for it. It never says who pays for that, and the 'who pays' parts under each option didn't show until tapped.
